title: Quantum Encoding and Analysis on Continuous Time Stochastic Process with Financial Applications
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a quantum algorithmic framework for continuous-time stochastic processes (QCTSP) composed of two main procedures: data preparation (encoding/compression) and information extraction (decoding/analysis). The encoding achieves exponential reductions in qubit number and circuit depth with respect to a holding-time parameter, while the extraction extends quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo to the continuous-time regime with a quadratic speedup and supports history-sensitive quantities. The framework is demonstrated on financial tasks including option pricing under the Merton Jump Diffusion model and ruin probability computation in a collective risk model.
methodology_description: This work develops an algorithmic framework for representing, preparing and extracting information from continuous-time stochastic processes (CTSPs) on a quantum computer. The authors introduce two compressed encodings for CTSP paths: a holding-time representation ((X_j, tau_j) pairs) and an increment representation ((Y_j, T_j) pairs). The QCTSP state is stored across three registers (index, data, time) as a superposition over discrete compressed path realizations with amplitude factorization consistent with the conditional structure of the process. They introduce the notion of memory length ML(X) to characterize the dependence of current state on past history and use it to analyze circuit depth and entanglement. For memory-less processes they show holding times are exponential and give a constant-depth preparation circuit; more complex families (Lévy processes, Poisson and compound Poisson processes, continuous-time Markov chains, Cox processes) are treated with dedicated circuits that exploit independence or conditional structure to reduce qubit count and depth. State preparation subroutines use Grover-style state preparation for arbitrary distributions, controlled multi-qubit rotations for exponential/truncated distributions, ripple-carry adders/subtractors for reconstructing cumulative states, and parallelized subcircuits where possible. For information extraction they map continuous integrals (e.g., I = ∫ X(t) dt or weighted integrals ∫ g(t)X(t) dt) to finite Riemann-sum forms (sums of Z_j = X_j tau_j or W_j = Y_j * G(T_j-1)), implement quantum multiplication via controlled rotations, approximate payoff/observable functions via periodic Fourier series, and evaluate Fourier expectation terms with controlled-rotation encodings plus Quantum Amplitude Estimation to obtain expected values with a quadratic speedup over classical Monte Carlo. History-sensitive queries (first hitting time) are implemented with an array of flag qubits, controlled subtractors and controlled flips to detect first crossing events along sampled pieces. The paper provides complexity bounds (qubits, circuit depth, gate counts) for each process class, proves several theorems about preparation and extraction, and demonstrates proof-of-principle simulations for Merton jump-diffusion option pricing and ruin probability in the collective risk model using the proposed circuits and parameter settings, showing consistency with analytic formulas where available.
algorithms_used: Fourier series approximation of payoff functions
key_findings: [theoretical] A framework (QCTSP) to encode continuous-time stochastic processes (CTSP) on quantum computers via two representations (holding-time and increment) that compress continuous paths into sequences of discrete random-variable pairs.

[theoretical] The compressed encoding yields an exponential reduction in qubit number and circuit depth with respect to the average holding time parameter τ_avg compared to uniform time-slicing: qubit count reduced from O(T log S) = O(n τ_avg log S) to O(n log(τ_avg S)), and circuit depth reduced from O(T log(nS)) to O(n log(nS)).

[theoretical] For memory-less (Markovian) holding times the holding time τ_j is exponential and can be prepared on ⌈log(-1/λ_j ln ε)⌉ qubits with constant circuit depth 1 (construction and proof provided).

[theoretical] Specific QCTSP subclasses (Poisson point process, compound Poisson, Lévy processes, continuous-time Markov chains, Cox processes) have explicit state-preparation circuits with stated complexity bounds (qubit counts, circuit depth, gate complexity) summarized (Table 2).

[theoretical] A method to evaluate continuous-time integrals (weightless integrals I(X,T) and time-weighted integrals J(X,T)) from the compressed encoding using controlled rotations, multipliers and Fourier/amplitude-estimation-based techniques, producing estimators with provable complexity.

[theoretical] The quantum-enhanced Monte Carlo (amplitude-estimation based) can be extended to continuous-time integrals and path-dependent quantities, yielding a quadratic speedup in sample complexity relative to classical Monte Carlo (error scaling from O(1/ε^2) to O(1/ε) in the usual setting).

[theoretical] History-sensitive quantities (e.g., first-hitting times, ruin events) can be extracted from the QCTSP encoding by introducing a sequence of flag qubits and controlled arithmetic operations to detect path-dependent events without requiring additional copies of the whole path.
[theoretical] The QCTSP preparation procedure does not require qRAM and can act as a modular subroutine for other quantum algorithms, partially mitigating the common data-input bottleneck.

[speculative] The authors claim QCTSP is well-suited to NISQ-era devices because of (i) lower qubit requirements, (ii) parallel preparation possibilities, and (iii) lower connectivity requirements in many instances; this claim is argued qualitatively but not demonstrated on hardware.

[supported] The proposed QCTSP method was used in classical simulations to price European call options in the Merton Jump Diffusion model; the simulation results reported are consistent with the truncated Merton analytic formula and with classical Monte Carlo.

[supported] The QCTSP method was used in classical simulations to estimate ultimate ruin probabilities in the Collective Risk Model; simulation results reported align with theoretical benchmarks and improve with longer sampled path lengths.

[speculative] The authors suggest that the framework can be generalized to many other CTSPs of financial relevance (e.g., Hawkes processes) and to broader applications (physics, biology, time-series), but those extensions are left for future work.

[speculative] Claims about practical hardware-efficiency (topology/connectivity metrics, experimental viability) are proposed as expected advantages but require further quantitative/experimental validation.
results_summary: This preprint introduces QCTSP, a theoretical quantum algorithmic framework to encode and analyze continuous-time stochastic processes using two compressed representations (holding-time and increment). The authors derive circuit constructions for several common CTSP families (Poisson, compound Poisson, Lévy, continuous-time Markov, Cox), proving asymptotic bounds for qubit counts, circuit depths and gate complexities. They extend amplitude-estimation-based quantum Monte Carlo to continuous-time integrals (including time-weighted and path-dependent quantities) and show how to extract history-sensitive events (e.g., first-hitting times) via flag qubits. Theoretical results claim exponential reductions in qubit and depth complexity with respect to average holding time and a quadratic sampling-speedup for Monte Carlo estimations. Classical simulations for option pricing under the Merton Jump Diffusion model and for ruin probability in a Collective Risk Model are reported and shown consistent with analytical benchmarks.
performance_claims: Qubit count reduction: from O(T log S) = O(n τ_avg log S) (uniform sampling) to O(n log(τ_avg S)) using QCTSP compressed encoding (exponential reduction in τ_avg).
Circuit depth reduction: from O(T log(nS)) = O(n τ_avg log(nS τ_avg)) (uniform sampling) to O(n log(nS)) using QCTSP encoding (exponential reduction in τ_avg).
Memory-less holding-time preparation: τ_j can be prepared on ⌈log(-1/λ_j ln ε)⌉ qubits with constant circuit depth 1 and gate complexity ⌈log(-1/λ_j ln ε)⌉.
Poisson process preparation: prepared on n⌈log(-n ln ε / λ)⌉ qubits with circuit depth ⌈log n⌉ and O(n⌈log(-n ln ε / λ)⌉) control-rotation gates (Corollary 3).
Compound Poisson process preparation: n⌈log(-nS ln ε / λ)⌉ qubits, circuit depth S + n⌈log(nS)⌉, gate complexity O(n⌈log(-nS ln ε / λ)⌉) (Corollary 4).
Lévy process upper bound: prepareable on n log(nS) qubits within O(S + n log(nS)) circuit depth and O(n(S + log(nS))) gate complexity (Theorem 2).
Continuous Markov process: preparable on n⌈log(-S ln ε / λ_min)⌉ qubits, circuit depth n S^2, and gate complexity O(n S ⌈S + log(-ln ε / λ_min)⌉) (Theorem 5).
Cox process: preparable on O(n(q_F + q_G - ln ε / |λ_min|)) qubits with circuit depth O(max{q_G, q_F + 2 d_F} + n q_G) in one representation (Theorem 6).

Continuous-time integral estimation (I(X,T) and J(X,T)): achievable with circuit depth O(P + n l_x l_τ) (holding-time representation) and time complexity scaling O(L P_ε (P + n l_x l_τ)), where amplitude estimation yields the 1/ε scaling.
Quadratic Monte Carlo speedup: extension of amplitude estimation to continuous-time integrals reducing sample complexity from classical O(1/ε^2) to O(1/ε) (claimed).

Classical simulations: reported option-pricing simulations (Merton Jump Diffusion) with parameters S0=100, K=100, r in {0.05,0.1,0.15}, σ=0.02, T=1, Δt=1/30, and multiple jump-parameter grids, showing consistency with truncated Merton formula (40 terms) and classical Monte Carlo (reported in figures).

Classical simulations: ruin probability simulations with λ_t=0.6, λ_ξ=1, c=1, ε=0.001, shot number 1000 per point, showing alignment with theoretical benchmarks and improved accuracy with increased path length (reported in figures).
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper claims provable algorithmic advantages: exponential reductions in qubit number and circuit depth with respect to the average holding time parameter via compressed encodings, and a quadratic Monte Carlo speedup for continuous-time integrals by extending amplitude estimation. These are complexity-theoretic constructions and proofs (no demonstrated hardware quantum speedup); limited classical simulations corroborate correctness for specific financial examples but do not constitute experimental quantum advantage.
limitations: No detailed quantitative analysis of hardware efficiency or topological/connectivity requirements for practical implementations (authors note this is lacking and left for future experimental demonstration).
The paper does not explore preparation procedures for many other practically relevant CTSPs (authors cite Hawkes processes as an example not studied).

Applications demonstrated are limited: only two financial examples (Merton Jump Diffusion option pricing and ruin probability) are implemented; many other finance and market-microstructure applications are not explored.

Extraction of path-dependent and history-sensitive information is sketched (flags, controlled subtractors) but a full theoretical analysis of these procedures (e.g., complexity, error, optimality) is left for future work.

Preparation of general Lévy processes ignores the compensated generalized Poisson part (Z_t) with infinitely many small jumps; the method truncates or omits this term, implying approximation error for processes with abundant small jumps.

For general Lévy processes the sampling-space size S and preparation of the underlying distribution F can be large, and the classical precomputation or classical cost to prepare F may be substantial (authors note this may consume enormous classical resources).

[inferred] State-preparation circuits rely on many multi-controlled rotations and adders; for processes with long memory length ML(X) the gate count and circuit depth grow rapidly (potentially exponentially), which may be prohibitive on near-term quantum hardware.
[inferred] The framework assumes a finite discretized state space S; discretization introduces approximation/truncation errors that are not fully quantified across use-cases.

[inferred] The amplitude-estimation based information-extraction relies on high-fidelity controlled rotations and many repetitions; noise and decoherence on NISQ devices could substantially reduce practical speedups.

[inferred] Many algorithmic steps require computation of precise rotation angles (for distributions, multipliers, Fourier approximations); classical precomputation and finite precision will introduce implementation overheads and numerical error that are not fully analyzed.

[inferred] Scalability limits: qubit counts, connectivity, and depth reductions are expressed asymptotically (in terms of τ_avg, n, S, etc.), but constant factors and actual resource requirements for practically relevant parameter regimes are not provided.

[inferred] The method often truncates infinite sums or distributions (e.g., truncating exponential tails); how truncation errors interact with amplitude estimation and final result accuracy is not fully characterized.
open_questions: How to quantitatively characterize the hardware efficiency (including circuit connectivity and topological constraints) of the proposed QCTSP circuits in realistic quantum devices?
Can the QCTSP preparation and extraction framework be extended efficiently to CTSP families not studied here (e.g., Hawkes processes) and what circuit constructions would be needed?
What are the precise complexity and error bounds (including constants) for extracting history-sensitive quantities such as first-hitting times using the flag-qubit approach?
How to best store and process history information for continuous quantum walks, and what is the relationship between continuous quantum walks and QCTSP-based financial models?
What is the impact of truncating compensated small-jump components (Z_t) of general Lévy processes on pricing and risk quantities, and can one bound the approximation error introduced?
How do discretization choices (state-space and time) and Fourier-series truncations interact with amplitude estimation to determine overall accuracy and required resources?

What are the practical NISQ-era performance and noise tolerance of the proposed circuits (state preparation, multipliers, controlled rotations, and amplitude estimation) for realistic financial instances?
How much classical precomputation is needed in realistic settings (rotation angles, distribution approximations), and does that classical cost offset the quantum advantages?
Can the framework be integrated with qRAM or other data-loading primitives to handle very large or streaming datasets, and what trade-offs would that introduce?
What are the optimal trade-offs between holding-time representation and increment representation in terms of qubit usage, circuit depth, and estimation error for various quantities of interest?

#idea:quantum-advantage — The framework implements history-sensitive path-dependent queries (e.g., first-hitting times, ruin events) using flag qubits and controlled arithmetic, avoiding full duplication of path states and enabling quantum evaluation of path-dependent observables.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The paper supplies explicit state-preparation circuits and complexity bounds for CTSP subclasses (Poisson, compound Poisson, Lévy, CTMC, Cox processes), showing how process conditional independence can reduce gate depth and qubit overhead.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The method combines classical preprocessing (Riemann-sum discretisation, Fourier-series approximation of payoffs) with quantum subroutines (distribution loading, controlled multipliers, amplitude estimation), making the approach modular and compatible with classical components.
